title: Nalanda burned
hook: around 1200 the great monasteries were sacked and burned; the libraries were lost

segments.voice: Yesterday, saddhamma fading in India. Your line was many reasons. Did you catch yourself reaching for just one? Today, one of those reasons, the hardest one to tell. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

A Tibetan pilgrim walks into the ruins of Nalanda. His name is Dharmasvamin, and the account of his travels, written down by a student, describes what he found: halls damaged and deserted, most of the monks gone. And in the middle of the ruins, an old teacher named Rahula Shribhadra, still teaching his students. Raiders had already come through. The account says they would come again while the pilgrim was there.
screen: `A PILGRIM IN THE RUINS.` → `AN OLD TEACHER, STILL TEACHING.` → `NALANDA BURNED.`

segments.voice: First, the raids. As armies conquered northern India, they attacked the great monasteries of the east. A Persian chronicle of the period describes soldiers storming what they took for a fortress, finding it full of books and shaven-headed men, and only afterward learning it had been a place of study. Historians debate which monastery that passage describes, and whether Nalanda fell in one attack or was damaged over years. Second, the libraries. These monasteries kept manuscripts copied by hand, on palm leaf and bark, and later accounts say the libraries burned. Some texts survived because monks carried them away, or because copies had already traveled to Tibet, Nepal or China. Some Buddhist works now survive only in translation, with no Sanskrit original known. Third, the people. Monks were killed or scattered, and some fled north into the mountains, carrying what they could. Fourth, the witness. The pilgrim's account shows that the place was not simply erased. A teacher still taught. A student still came. When the soldiers returned, the account says, the old teacher would not leave, and the pilgrim carried him on his back to a hiding place, and they waited until the danger passed. Then they went on with the lessons. The tradition teaches impermanence. Here it is in smoke and ash: generations of learning gone, and an old teacher and his student, back at the books.
screen: `A CHRONICLE: A FORT FULL OF BOOKS.` · `THE LIBRARIES BURN.` · `MONKS FLEE NORTH.` · `THE PILGRIM CARRIES HIS TEACHER.` · then, large: `BACK AT THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one lost library. Settle, and let the breath slow. Think of something written or remembered that is gone: a letter thrown away, a recipe nobody wrote down, a grandparent's stories no one recorded, or a library you've only read about. Hold it in mind. With each breath, honor it: the hands that made it, the people who read it. Then, if you like, choose one thing you could write down this week so it isn't lost. The bell holds the time.
Nalanda burned. The raids that sacked the great monasteries of eastern India and burned their libraries, while some monks and some books escaped. Today's word.
Your line: the libraries burned. Today, save one thing worth keeping: write down a family story, back up a photo, copy out a recipe. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember the destruction of the great Indian monasteries in teaching and pilgrimage, and the ruins of Nalanda are visited today by pilgrims and students from across the Buddhist world.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the name of the great monastery of eastern India.

trapdoor: what you thought: one fire, one night, everything gone.
what it means: raids sacked the monasteries and burned libraries, but some people and some books survived.
what a scholar hears: a Persian chronicle describes soldiers seizing a monastery full of books, historians debate which one, and a Tibetan pilgrim's account shows teaching went on in the ruins.

notes: Index hook says 'around 1200'; the date is left out of the spoken script under the claims rule. Keeper may restore it if a cited source is added.

Dharmasvamin details (account written by a student; Rahula Shribhadra teaching a small group; soldiers returning; pilgrim carrying his teacher to hiding) follow the biography as translated by Roerich; please verify each beat.
Persian chronicle (Tabaqat-i Nasiri) paraphrased; the monastery it describes is usually identified with Odantapuri, not Nalanda, so the script says historians debate which one. Confirm.
'Some Buddhist works survive only in translation, with no Sanskrit original known': general; confirm.
Tone: violence described plainly without naming a religion or people as villains; confirm this is fair and careful.
Editor: replaced the superlative 'impermanence at its hardest' with a concrete close; cut the templated 'Today, Nalanda burned' hook ending.

Auditor: 'a small group of students' cut ('small' is not supported: the Roerich translation of the biography gives about seventy); 'one young one' changed to 'his student', since Dharmasvamin was a mature monk, not a youth, at the time of the visit. Keeper may verify both against the biography.
